'''Maggie Hall Miller''' (born in 1993 or 1994<ref>[https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=7286 News from the AMS, Sharing Research, Making Connections: A Tale of Two Mathematicians at JMM, January 29, 2024] (Note: ''News from the AMS'' says "She is just 30", in 2024)</ref>) is a mathematician whose primary area of research is [[low-dimensional topology]]. She is an assistant professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. She is known for work on [[Seifert surface]]s, including a 2022 result with Kyle Hayden, Seungwon Kim, JungHwan Park and Isaac Sundberg that answered a 1982 question of [[Charles Livingston (mathematician)|Charles Livingston]] by constructing Seifert surfaces for a knot that remain non‑isotopic in the 4‑ball; the paper was published in 2025 in the ''[[Journal of the European Mathematical Society]]''.<ref name=jems2025>{{cite journal |last1=Hayden |first1=Kyle |last2=Kim |first2=Seungwon |last3=Miller |first3=Maggie |last4=Park |first4=JungHwan |last5=Sundberg |first5=Isaac |title=Seifert surfaces in the 4-ball |journal=Journal of the European Mathematical Society |date=2025-09-29 |doi=10.4171/JEMS/1703 |url=https://ems.press/journals/jems/articles/14299167 |arxiv=2205.15283}}</ref><ref name=quanta>{{cite magazine |last=Hartnett |first=Kevin |title=Surfaces So Different Even a Fourth Dimension Can't Make Them the Same |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/special-surfaces-remain-distinct-in-four-dimensions-20220616/ |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |date=2022-06-16 |access-date=2025-11-17}}</ref> Her honors include the [[Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics#Maryam_Mirzakhani_New_Frontiers_Prize|Maryam Mirzakhani New Frontiers Prize]] (2023), a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]] (2025), and a [[Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering]] (2025).<ref>{{Cite web |title=2025 Fellows |url=https://sloan.org/fellowships/2025-Fellows |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Maggie Miller |url=https://www.packard.org/fellow/maggie-miller/ |website=The David and Lucile Packard Foundation |access-date=2025-11-17}}</ref>

==Contributions to mathematics==
In 2022, together with Kyle Hayden, Seungwon Kim, JungHwan Park and Isaac Sundberg, Miller answered a 1982 [[question]] of [[Charles Livingston (mathematician)|Charles Livingston]] on [[Seifert surface]]s by exhibiting surfaces for the same knot that remain non‑isotopic when their interiors are pushed into the 4‑ball. The results include examples that are not even topologically isotopic in the 4‑ball, examples that are topologically but not smoothly isotopic, and infinite families distinct up to isotopy rel. boundary. The work was published in the ''[[Journal of the European Mathematical Society]]'' in 2025.<ref name=jems2025/><ref name=quanta/>

==Education and career==
Miller completed her undergraduate studies at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Maggie Miller – Women In Math |url=https://math.mit.edu/wim/members/maggie-miller/ |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=math.mit.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Maggie Miller, Mathematics |date=2015-05-11 |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/utcns/17828966055/|publisher=University of Texas College of Natural Sciences|via=Flickr |access-date=2022-03-12}}</ref>

She earned her PhD in mathematics from [[Princeton University]] in 2020, with [[David Gabai]] as advisor (thesis: ''Extending fibrations of knot complements to ribbon disk complements'').<ref>{{Cite web |title=Princeton University Doctoral Dissertations: Extending fibrations of knot complements to ribbon disk complements |url=https://arks.princeton.edu/ark:/88435/dsp01w6634654p |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=Princeton DataSpace}}</ref><ref>{{mathgenealogy|264868}}</ref>

After completing her doctoral degree, Miller worked as an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Postdoctoral Fellow from 2020 to 2021 at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":1" /> Later as a Visiting Clay Fellow and Stanford Science Fellow, she spent time at [[Stanford University]] from 2021 to 2023.<ref name=ssf>{{Cite web |title=Meet the Fellows |work=Science Fellows |publisher=Stanford University|url=https://stanfordsciencefellows.stanford.edu/meet-fellows |access-date=2022-03-12 |language=en}}</ref> Miller is currently a tenure track professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Hartnett |first=Kevin |date=2024-02-22 |title=A New Agenda for Low-Dimensional Topology |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-new-agenda-for-low-dimensional-topology-20240222/ |access-date=2024-03-18 |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=CNS Welcomes New Faculty for the 23-24 Academic Year {{!}} College of Natural Sciences |url=https://cns.utexas.edu/news/announcements/cns-welcomes-new-faculty-23-24-academic-year |access-date=2024-04-05 |website=cns.utexas.edu |language=en}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Miller was awarded a 2021 Clay Research Fellowship by the [[Clay Mathematics Institute]] for her work to expand topological research of [[manifold]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=May 2021 |title=Mathematics People |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202105/rnoti-p824.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |volume=68 |pages=828–829}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2021 Clay Research Fellows {{!}} Clay Mathematics Institute |url=https://claymath.org/events/news/2021-clay-research-fellows |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=claymath.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Maggie Miller *20 and Georgios Moschidis *18 Named 2021 Clay Research Fellows {{!}} Math |url=https://www.math.princeton.edu/news/maggie-miller-20-and-georgios-moschidis-18-named-2021-clay-research-fellows |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=www.math.princeton.edu}}</ref> Her contributions were described by MIT as "important...to long-standing problems in low-dimensional topology."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lisa Piccirillo and Postdoc Maggie Miller Named 2021 Clay Research Fellows – Women In Math |url=https://math.mit.edu/wim/2021/04/07/lisa-piccirillo-and-postdoc-maggie-miller-named-2021-clay-research-fellows/ |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=math.mit.edu}}</ref> Clay Research Fellowships are awarded to recent PhD-holders who are selected for their research accomplishments and potential as leaders in mathematics research.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellowship Nominations {{!}} Clay Mathematics Institute |url=https://www.claymath.org/programs/fellowship-nominations |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=www.claymath.org}}</ref>

In her previous position at Stanford, she was a Stanford Science Fellow.<ref name=ssf/> Fellowships are awarded to early career scientists who have demonstrated scientific achievement and advancement, as well as a desire to collaborate with a diverse scholarly community.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Science Fellows |url=https://stanfordsciencefellows.stanford.edu/ |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=stanfordsciencefellows.stanford.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Apply {{!}} Science Fellows |url=https://stanfordsciencefellows.stanford.edu/apply |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=stanfordsciencefellows.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Prior to her appointment at Stanford, Miller was awarded a [[National Science Foundation]] Mathematical Sciences Postdoc Research Fellowship while at MIT in the Department of Mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NSF Award Search: Award # 2001675 - PostDoctoral Research Fellowship |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2001675&HistoricalAwards=false |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=www.nsf.gov |language=en}}</ref> She also has a record of accomplishment during her graduate studies, having been awarded the Princeton Mathematics Graduate Teaching Award in 2018 and the Charlotte Elizabeth Procter Fellowship in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Boumal, Miller, Nestoridi Receive Department Teaching Awards {{!}} Math |url=https://www.math.princeton.edu/news/boumal-miller-nestoridi-receive-department-teaching-awards |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=www.math.princeton.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Honorific Fellowship Award Winners {{!}} Graduate School |url=https://gradschool.princeton.edu/about/awards |access-date=2022-03-12 |website=gradschool.princeton.edu}}</ref>

She received the 2023 [[Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics#Maryam_Mirzakhani_New_Frontiers_Prize|Maryam Mirzakhani New Frontiers Prize]], one of the [[Breakthrough Prize]]s, for "work on fibered ribbon knots and surfaces in 4-dimensional manifolds.",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/3/L3927|title=Breakthrough Prize – Mathematics Breakthrough Prize Laureates – Maggie Miller|website=breakthroughprize.org}}</ref> and was named one of [[Forbes]]' 30 Under 30 – Science for 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Maggie Miller |url=https://www.forbes.com/profile/maggie-miller/ |access-date=2024-03-18 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

In 2025, Miller was awarded a Sloan Research Fellowship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2025 Fellows {{!}} Alfred P. Sloan Foundation |url=https://sloan.org/fellowships/2025-Fellows |access-date=2025-04-04 |website=sloan.org |language=en}}</ref> In the same year, she received a [[Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The David and Lucile Packard Foundation Announces the 2025 Class of Packard Fellows for Science and Engineering |url=https://www.packard.org/insights/news/the-david-and-lucile-packard-foundation-announces-the-2025-class-of-packard-fellows-for-science-and-engineering/ |website=packard.org |date=2025-10-15 |access-date=2025-11-17}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Maggie Miller |url=https://www.packard.org/fellow/maggie-miller/ |website=packard.org |access-date=2025-11-17}}</ref>

She delivered a lecture titled ''Constructing Fibrations in 4D'' at the 2026 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]].<ref name="ICM">https://www.icm2026.org/event/ac193975-5d24-4628-8c30-ddb23de19a8b/speakers</ref>
